LESSON 84 OF 106·Offensive Thinking and Safe Testing

Scanners, Benchmarks and Interpreting a Report

Why automated output is a list of claims rather than a list of findings, how a benchmark differs from a risk, and the four questions that turn an item into work somebody can schedule.

Applied Foundation15 min
Why this matters

A scanner tells you what matches a signature. A benchmark tells you what should be configured. Neither tells you whether your system is actually attackable, and a report of several thousand findings is usually a measurement problem rather than a security one.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Scanners compare configuration and version data against a signature set, so they find what has been written down.
  • Benchmarks are curated configuration guidance for a platform, usually hardened defaults with justification.
  • A scan finding is evidence of a possible weakness, not evidence of a vulnerability, until someone confirms it.
  • The highest-value findings are the small number that combine with something else to create a path.
  • Coverage matters more than count: a scan of the wrong network tells you nothing about the right one.

The background

  • Network scanners were the original tool, and made regular scanning a routine part of administration.
  • Web application scanners matured into the dominant source of application findings.
  • Configuration benchmarks were written to give administrators a defensible target rather than an opinion.
  • Continuous and agent-based scanning moved the model from scheduled sweeps to live visibility.

Real-world examples

  • A report of four thousand findings gets triaged to about ten, and the rest is discarded, which is a wasted exercise.
  • A high-severity finding on a host with no route from the internet is a lower real risk than a medium one on a public host.
  • A scan that only covers unauthenticated checks misses the misconfigurations that are actually found in the wild.

What to look for

  • Check whether authenticated scanning was used, since unauthenticated checks see very little.
  • Check whether the report distinguishes confirmed findings from informational items.
  • Check whether severity accounts for exposure and not only for the technical severity of the issue.
  • Check the scan date and whether the estate has changed since.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Reading how a published guide separates the techniques that generate findings from the analysis and mitigation work that makes them actionable

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Use authenticated scanning, and make the credential a managed one with read-only access where possible.
  • Tune the signature set to your estate so the report reflects your technology.
  • Convert a scan into a work queue by grouping findings by control rather than by tool.
  • Verify high-severity findings by hand before acting, since scanners produce false positives at every severity.
  • Rescan continuously and alert on the change, rather than reading a monthly report.
